title: MathEDU: Feedback Generation on Problem-Solving Processes for Mathematical Learning Support
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative AI systems can reliably assess students’ mathematical problem-solving processes and generate useful feedback, rather than only producing a correct final answer. The authors focus on three linked tasks: classifying whether a student’s answer is correct, identifying the specific step where an error occurs, and generating teacher-like feedback that explains the mistake and suggests how to improve.

To study these questions, the authors construct MathEDU, a dataset extending MathQA with 4,048 real student solutions and teacher-written annotations. Six university students solved a balanced sample of GRE-level math word problems drawn from six MathQA categories, and three mathematics education experts annotated errors, error categories, and feedback. The study then evaluates several LLMs, including Llama3 8B, Llama3 70B, GPT-3.5, o1-mini, and fine-tuned Llama3 8B variants using LoRA under single-task, multi-task, and end-to-end setups, with and without the original rationales.

Results show that larger models and fine-tuned models can do reasonably well on answer correctness classification, especially when rationales are available, but identifying exact error steps is substantially harder. Feedback generation is the most difficult task: model outputs are often verbose, imprecise, or misaligned with teacher feedback, and sometimes they misdiagnose correct work or provide judgmental wording. The authors conclude that current generative AI systems still lack the pedagogy-aware reliability needed for trustworthy educational feedback, and that future systems need better understanding of student reasoning, more precise diagnosis, and more supportive language.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of large language models used for grading, error identification, and feedback generation in mathematical problem-solving tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as few-shot prompting baselines and as the base model for LoRA fine-tuning (Llama3 8B and Llama3 70B) to classify answer correctness, identify erroneous steps, and generate teacher-like feedback for student math solutions.

findings.finding_summary: Llama3 models varied by size and input rationale. For answer correctness classification, Llama3 70B achieved 88.23% F-score without rationale and 86.65% with rationale, while Llama3 8B improved from 66.96% to 77.04% when rationale was added. Fine-tuned end-to-end models reached 92.09%-94.38% F-score depending on rationale, with the best single-task model reaching 95.07% F-score.
findings.sample_size: n=603 test examples (answer correctness classification test set)

findings.finding_summary: For error identification, Llama3 8B achieved 28.40% exact match (EM) without rationale and 11.73% with rationale; Llama3 70B achieved 32.10% EM without rationale and 29.63% with rationale. Human-reviewed discussion in the paper indicates rationale sometimes reduced performance because of format mismatch, and fine-tuned end-to-end models with rationale performed better than baseline Llama3 8B.
findings.measure: Exact match and Hausdorff distance for error-span identification
findings.sample_size: n=603 test examples (overall), with error-identification evaluated on incorrect solutions

findings.finding_summary: In feedback generation, Llama3 8B obtained ROUGE-L 0.2391 without rationale and 0.1632 with rationale, BERTScore 0.7654 without rationale and 0.5515 with rationale, and an LLM rating of 2.68 without rationale and 2.14 with rationale. Human evaluation found all models remained below the ideal score of 3, with Llama3 70B sometimes producing judgmental phrasing that could discourage students.
findings.measure: ROUGE-L, BERTScore, GPT-4-based LLM rating, and human ratings of feedback quality
findings.sample_size: n=603 test examples; human evaluation on representative outputs

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used here for correctness classification, feedback generation, and as an automated evaluator of generated feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as GPT-3.5 on grading and feedback tasks; additionally GPT-4 was used as the LLM judge for automatic feedback evaluation, and GPT-4o was used in the automated characterization of feedback errors.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3.5 underperformed the LLaMA models on correctness classification, with F-score 33.83% without rationale and 49.92% with rationale. The paper notes GPT-3.5 often judged answers as incorrect if intermediate steps were omitted, even when final answers were right.

For error identification, GPT-3.5 achieved 30.25% EM without rationale and 27.78% with rationale, with Hausdorff distance 63.72 and 60.80, respectively. For feedback generation, GPT-3.5 obtained ROUGE-L 0.2695 without rationale and 0.2597 with rationale, BERTScore 0.8395 and 0.8366, and LLM ratings of 3.70 and 3.63.
findings.measure: Exact match/Hausdorff distance for error identification; ROUGE-L, BERTScore, and GPT-4-based LLM rating for feedback generation

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study with annotated data and comparative model evaluation, but it is not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful yet limited by single-dataset, single-domain design and model-comparison methodology.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial performance differences across models and tasks, but it does not provide causal effect sizes or intervention impacts on learners or teachers. Results are informative about model capability and risk, but the educational impact remains indirect and task-specific.
